mcqs.question: What makes "narrate the exact interleaving" the actual answer, rather than just naming that a race exists?
options: It's required by the Java Language Specification for any race-condition explanation
It proves the bug can never occur in production, since it's been narrated
It's only useful for races involving exactly two threads, never more
It shows you found the specific gap between two operations and can explain precisely how two threads break the invariant, not just that shared state exists
mcqs.explanation: Naming the exact interleaving demonstrates you located the real gap, not just noticed shared state — that specificity is what's actually graded. There's no such language-spec requirement, narration doesn't prove anything about production behavior, and the technique applies to races among any number of threads.

mcqs.question: In the lazy-initialization Cache example, what's the actual race?
options: Two threads can both see data as null, both call loadFromDisk(), and both assign a result — wasting work and potentially double-triggering any side effects
The Map interface itself is not allowed to be used as a field type
loadFromDisk() throws an exception whenever called from two threads
The get() method cannot be called more than once per object lifetime
mcqs.explanation: The check-then-construct-then-assign sequence isn't atomic, so two threads can both pass the null check before either finishes constructing, duplicating work and side effects. Map is a perfectly valid field type, loadFromDisk() has no such restriction, and get() can be called any number of times.

mcqs.question: Why doesn't synchronizing only hasNext() (leaving next() unsynchronized) fix the check-then-act race?
options: Because Java requires exactly two synchronized methods per class, no more or fewer
Because a lock only blocks other threads that also try to acquire that same lock — an unsynchronized method on the other side of the race can still run concurrently
Because hasNext() must always be private to be synchronized correctly
Because synchronizing only one method makes the other method throw a compile error
mcqs.explanation: A lock only serializes callers that acquire it; an unsynchronized next() never contends for that lock and can still run at the same time, defeating the fix. There's no rule about synchronized-method counts, method visibility, or a compile error here.

mcqs.question: Why is synchronizing only the reading method, while leaving the writing method unsynchronized, an incomplete fix?
options: Because reads are always faster than writes regardless of synchronization
Because Java automatically synchronizes all writes to any field that has a synchronized getter
An unsynchronized writer can still run concurrently with the synchronized reader, since the writer never contends for the same lock
Because the writing method would need to be declared static instead
mcqs.explanation: Synchronization only serializes against other synchronized callers on the same lock — an unsynchronized writer is free to run at the same time as the synchronized reader, leaving the race fully intact. Java has no such auto-synchronization rule, and static declaration is unrelated.
